|| Hitopadesha ||

->|| 140 ||<-

If war has indeed arrived, O King, why did you not prepare for it earlier? For, what kind of servant or minister is he who, without thought, advises a king to initiate the preparations for war and abandon his own position? Furthermore, one should always endeavor to conquer an enemy through means other than war, for when two parties are engaged in battle, the outcome is never certain. Moreover, one should attempt to overcome an enemy using conciliation, bribery, or dissension, either together or separately, but never by war. Additionally, every person is a hero as long as they have not yet encountered war; who would not be proud when the strength of the opponent remains unseen? Furthermore, a great result is not easily obtained by violent means when only minor measures are employed. However, having seen that war has arrived, one must treat the enemy with disregard. For,

<note>The Chakravaka bird, seeing the battle at hand, says: "O Great King, war should not be undertaken first. For, what kind of servant or minister is he who, without deliberation, advises a king to prepare for battle and abandon his own station? Moreover, one should strive to conquer an opponent through conciliation and other peaceful means, rather than through conflict, because when two sides are fighting, it is never certain who will emerge victorious. Additionally, one should attempt to resolve the matter with the enemy through conciliation, gifts, or sowing dissension, either individually or in combination, but never through war. Furthermore, everyone is a hero until they have actually fought, as no one knows the true strength of the other."</note>

<summary>This page discusses the folly of engaging in war, advising kings to prefer diplomacy, conciliation, and strategic maneuvering over military conflict due to the unpredictability of battle.</summary>
